October 30, 2026Analysis
AI models tend to draw more complaints the longer they’re out
We looked at a random sample of 100,000 replies users wrote in DesignArena chats from April through July 2026 and compared each of 80 models with itself. 70 of the 80 drew more complaints in June and July than in April and May. The rise held with the task, the language, the point in the chat, how long each user had been using DesignArena’s chat, and the length of the request all held fixed. It was led by complaints that an output fell short of what the user asked for, while complaints that something broke didn’t rise.

How Thinking Can Hurt One-Shot Websites and Games
Does a model build better websites and games when it thinks longer? We compared the two highest reasoning effort levels of Muse Spark 1.3 from Meta, Xhigh and Max, on prompts that both settings answered on DesignArena. In a sample of about 800 website and game prompts, Max thought about a third longer than Xhigh on the websites and nearly twice as long on the games.

How Being Opinionated Gives GPT-6 Astra an Edge
What should a model do with the image you give it? Most models treat a user’s reference image as a blueprint and reuse its colours, its layout, and sometimes the image itself. When does taste become slop?
Has beige serif become the new purple gradient? We analyzed tens of thousands of websites generated with DesignArena from January through October 2026, and we were surprised to find that some familiar styles have gained favor since the start of the year while others have lost it. Introducing Micro Evals
An overview of our live skills assessment methodology.
What are Micro Evals?
The current bottleneck in model progress isn’t figuring out how to improve models—it’s knowing what needs improvement. Creating realistic coding tasks for training or RL environments is difficult when you don’t know where models actually fail. Most data efforts rely on synthetic or reverse-engineered examples, which often produce inflated results on contrived codebases that bear little resemblance to real-world use.

In pursuit of a benchmark for human taste
We know when we like something, but when asked why, we stumble over our words and hallucinate reasoning. We contradict ourselves—we don’t know why we like a thing, we just do.
There exist people who understand our preferences better than we do ourselves. Let’s call them Tastemakers. Tastemakers know what we really want, not just what we say we want. Not a faster horse; a car. Great taste is a marker of how well we are understood.
